summary: A case is the form a noun phrase takes to show its role in the sentence. German has four: nominative (Nominativ), accusative (Akkusativ), dative (Dativ) and genitive (Genitiv). The case shows mostly on the article, much less on the noun: der Tisch – den Tisch – dem Tisch – des Tisches. The first one is the nominative: the form of the subject – the one who does something or is something – and of the noun after sein (Das ist ein Tisch. Er ist ein Freund.). It is also the dictionary form. To find the subject, ask Wer oder was …? (Who or what …?): Wer ist hier? – Der Lehrer. → der Lehrer is the subject, in the nominative.

blocks.title: Both sides of sein are nominative
blocks.text: Der Mann ist ein Lehrer. Das ist der Schlüssel. sein links two nominatives – it never takes an accusative (not *Das ist den Schlüssel).

blocks.title: Only the masculine gives it away
blocks.text: In the nominative and accusative, die and das look the same; only the masculine changes: der Tisch (subject) → den Tisch (object, S07). That is why German teachers drill the masculine.

askYourself: Who or what does it, or is it? Ask “Wer oder was …?” – the answer is the subject, in the nominative.
Is the noun after sein (Das ist …, Er ist …)? Then it is nominative too.
What gender and number does the noun have? → der / die / das / die; ein / eine / ein / –.
Is it a pronoun? ich, du, er, sie, es, wir, ihr, sie, Sie are the nominative forms.
Is the subject not in first place (Hier ist der Schlüssel)? It is still the subject – find the verb and ask Wer oder was?
steps: Ask Wer oder was + verb? → the subject.
Give its article the nominative form for its gender and number.

traps: The subject does not have to come first: in Hier ist der Schlüssel and Dort ist die Lampe, der Schlüssel and die Lampe are the subjects.
After sein there is no accusative: Er ist ein guter Freund, not *einen guten Freund.
die and das look the same in the nominative and accusative – only der → den shows the difference.
The dictionary form of a noun (der Tisch, die Lampe) is the nominative singular.

quiz.q: How many cases does German have?
Which case is the subject in?
quiz.why: The subject – who or what does or is something – is nominative.
Wer oder was ist hier? – Der Schlüssel.

quiz.q: Hier ist der Schlüssel. – Which words are the subject?
quiz.why: Wer oder was ist hier? – der Schlüssel (the subject need not come first).
After sein the nominative: ein Tisch (masculine).

seeAlso.note: Arabic has three cases, marked by short vowel endings (iʿrāb); the nominative ends in -u (al-baytu, baytun), usually not written.
Hebrew nouns have no cases; the role shows by word order, prepositions and et before a definite object.
Chinese has no cases: word order shows who does what (我看他 / 他看我).
The accusative (den, einen) – the direct object – comes at S07.

notes.text: Cases are familiar (ο δρόμος, τον δρόμο, του δρόμου), and the noun after είναι is nominative as in German. Greek shows the case on the noun ending as well; German mostly on the article. German has a dative, which Greek lacks.

Russian has six cases and shows them on the noun ending (стол, стола, столу); German has four and shows them mostly on the article. The nominative after “to be” is the same (Это стол – Das ist ein Tisch).
Spanish nouns have no cases (only pronouns: yo, me, mí); German shows the case on the article: der Tisch, den Tisch, dem Tisch, des Tisches.
English shows case only in pronouns (he – him); German shows it on the article too: der Tisch – den Tisch.
French marks case only in pronouns (il, le, lui); German marks it on every article.

Hindi nouns have a direct and an oblique form plus postpositions (laṛkā, laṛke ko), and in the perfective past a transitive subject takes ne (laṛke ne khānā khāyā). A German subject is always nominative, in every tense: Der Junge hat gegessen.
Persian has no case endings (only rā for a definite object); German shows the case on the article.
Marathi marks case with endings and postpositions on the noun, and in the perfective past a transitive subject takes -ne. A German subject is always in the nominative, whatever the tense.

Arabic nominative -u, accusative -a, genitive -i (al-kitābu, al-kitāba, al-kitābi) are the same idea; German has a fourth case, the dative, and shows the case mostly on the article. In a nominal sentence both nouns are nominative in Arabic too.
Hebrew nouns have no cases (only et before a definite object); German shows four cases on the article.
Turkish cases are suffixes on the noun (ev, evi, eve, evde, evden, evin), and the nominative has none (yalın hal); German marks even the nominative, on der / ein.
Japanese marks roles with particles after the noun (ga, o, ni); German changes the article. The topic (wa) is not a case: a German subject is nominative wherever it stands.
Korean marks the subject with i / ga, the object with eul / reul and the topic with eun / neun; German changes the article instead, and has no topic marker.
Finnish has fifteen cases on the noun, German four on the article. The predicate noun of olla is nominative in both (Hän on opettaja – Er ist Lehrer).
Many case suffixes, the nominative without any; German has only four cases, shown mostly on the article (der, den, dem, des).
Swahili has no cases: word order and the verb prefixes show who does what. German changes the article for the role: der Mann, den Mann.
Luganda nouns have no case forms; roles show in word order and the verb. German shows them on the article.
Chinese has no cases; word order shows the roles. German changes the article and can therefore move the object first (Den Tisch kaufe ich).
No cases in Vietnamese, word order decides; German marks roles on the article.

Inuktitut is ergative: the subject of a transitive verb takes its own case, while the subject of an intransitive verb looks like an object. German puts every subject in the nominative: Der Mann schläft. Der Mann kauft den Tisch.
